utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar, and welcome back. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here, and I think we are full house Defence teams; and Prosecution, I only see Mr. Thayer today. Any preliminaries? None? Good afternoon to you, sir. You are most welcome to this Tribunal where you are -- and to this case where you are going to give evidence very soon. Before you start doing so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth. Madam usher is going to give you the text of the declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. What is going to happen is Mr. Nikolic from the Beara Defence team that have summoned you as a Defence witness will be asking you a series of questions. He will then be followed by others on cross-examination, and after that you can go home. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As you know, I am Predrag Nikolic, and I represent the accused Beara together with my team, and I will be leading you today on behalf of the Defence team. First of all, could you please state your name for the record; also, could you tell us where you were born and your father's name?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Mikajlo Mitrovic. My father's name is Bogodan. I was born on the 22nd July, 1955, in the village of Zelena in the municipality of Zvornik, which was then the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I'm married. I have two children, and I reside in Banja Luka at number 50 Skena Koljnevica Street. My ID number is 22079555005013.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mitrovic. You provided us with quite a lot of details. Could you please tell us something about your educational background?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I completed the technical military academy in Zagreb. Upon completing the academy, I became the engineer of electronics, and I became a lieutenant by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is your current occupation, Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I'm retired, and I am also a post-graduate student at the school of philosophy in Banja Luka at the department of contemporary sociology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now let's go back to the period when you just completed your academy education. Where was your first posting?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: When I graduated in 1979, I was sent to work at the Postojna garrison in Slovenia as an official in the technical services, first in the logistics of the garrison and then in the technical department of the division command at Postojna barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you slowly give us all the assignments that you had until you retired?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I started working in 1979 at Postojna, and I stayed with the technical organ until 1983, and then I joined the security organ upon the proposal of the chief of security of the so-called 9th army and with the approval of the then-commander. I remained working in the security department of the division, and there I also worked as one of the desk officers. I also worked at various battalions as a desk officer and then in the security department of the division. You wanted to know more?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: In 1985, due to my child's illness I was re-assigned to work in the Sibenik garrison where I occupied the post of a desk officer in the 8th naval sector. This was for a year or two, and then I was the chief of the security department of the 11th brigade of the naval infantry in Sibenik, and on the eve of the war in Croatia I was appointed the chief of the department of the naval military district for counterintelligence. This is where I was when the war in Croatia started. In the course of the war in Croatia, I was injured in Sibenik and I was captured. I spent 45 days in a solitary cell in the Sibenik prison. Then on the 2nd of November, 1991, I was exchanged and was re-assigned to the Knin garrison where I was appointed the chief of the counterintelligence group of the 9th Knin corps. After that, I was also assigned to the Drvar garrison, and I was appointed the chief of the intelligence and security department of the 2nd Krajina corps. I remained in that position from the moment the corps was established to the moment when it was disbanded. After the war, I worked as the deputy chief of the counterintelligence group of the Army Republika Srpska, and then in 1998 I was appointed the assistant Minister of Defence of Republika Srpska in charge of security and intelligence, and from there I was pensioned off in 2002. That would be my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This was, again, providing us with a lot of details, but let's go back to some of them. Mr. Mitrovic, when did you first meet Colonel Beara, actually, Ljubisa Beara as he was then?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: He was the brigade captain, and I met him sometime in 1985. I said that that year I was re-assigned to the Sibenik garrison, and when he came to control and tour the security organs of the 8th naval military district, obviously, I reported to him because he was my superior, and that's when I actually met him for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one small correction. On page 22, line 14, could you please repeat -- page 4, line 22. Could you please tell us the exact rank that Ljubisa Beara held at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: He was a captain, which would be the rank of a colonel in the land forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What was the position of Mr. Beara at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: At the time, he was the assistant chief of the security department of the naval district, and by establishment he was also the deputy chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Given your position and given his position, what was your relationship in terms of subordination?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Captain Beara was my second superior. I was a desk officer. I had my chief, at the time I was captain 1st class, as far as I can remember, and that would be the relationship between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How often did you have an opportunity to meet Mr. Beara while you were serving in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to give you any numbers, if you wanted me to give you numbers. In any case, several times a year, at least four to five times a year in Sibenik itself. But there were also occasions when Captain Beara would summon us to come to the command, to the naval district, i.e., to the seat of the security department of the naval district. That's when we had to go to meet him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what was the ethnic composition of your unit and especially the security organ during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: You have to bear in mind that the army was still the JNA and that the JNA effectively reflected the ethnic composition of the then-state. As far as the security organ is concerned, there were representatives of all ethnic groups starting with Albanians. One of the organs of security at the time was Rahim Ademy, the current general of the Croatian army. There were also Croats, Macedonians, Muslim Serbs, of course, Montenegrins, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please make a pause after my question?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now, based on your official contacts and relationship with Mr. Beara, what was your opinion of him as an officer, as a professional serving in the same military?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Naval Captain Beara in our eyes was a role model in professional terms. He was a professional, an exceptional professional. He adhered to the legality of work - that was his main concern - and he was a professional in terms of providing professional guidance to the security organs, especially when it came to counterintelligence. He was also a professional when it came to the subordination relationship. He was primarily a person who understood issues and human problems that we all had, more or less, and his appearance was also something that commanded respect, especially when he wore a uniform. He is an extremely intelligent and educated person, and what he had were manners of a true gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: One must admit that it's very nice to hear these words; however, are there any facts that may corroborate what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I can illustrate this by giving you an example that concerns the protection of the legality of our work; for example, in the course of 1991, i.e. towards the end of that year, when the units and the command of the 8th naval district were in Sibenik encircled by the paramilitary forces of the Republic of Croatia at the time, the ZNG. I was one of those who experienced that encirclement, and we experienced all sorts of provocations, ill-treatment, and so on and so forth. Every day, civilian population would be brought to our facilities as a human shield, and in addition to that huge loudspeakers were mounted up in the winery next to the barracks and they played loud music. They would try to talk the recruits serving in the army to desert the facilities, and the officers, they also brought their wives and the children of the officers who were trapped in the barracks. They persuaded him to talk to their fathers and husbands and to try to talk them into deserting, and this went on for 24 hours a day for ten or even -- ten days or even longer. We asked from naval Captain Beara for his permission to destroy those loudspeakers. We had automatic pistols with silencers with which we could do it; however, he refused to approve that because according to him this would have been a provocation which might have led to incidents and that this might have given a reason to ZNG to open fire on us, which would probably result in the deaths of soldiers and officers, let alone civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, at that time which rules and regulations did you apply; i.e., what regulations and laws was your work based on?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about that time, we are talking about the law on defence, the rules and regulations of the work in the JNA, and all the other rules that were in effect; and when it comes to the security organ, then we were talking about the rules of service of the security organ in the then-JNA, which had a legal effect at the time; and we are also talking about the guidance or instruction on the application of the methods and works of the security organs. We are also talking about the rules of service of the military police and the instruction on deliberation of the rules for the work of the military police. Those were the legal documents that we used in our everyday work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In view of all that you've just told us and the rules that governed your work, I would like to hear your opinion. In the situation that you've just mentioned and in the face of provocations of the paramilitaries, did you have legal means to use weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the situation threatened the security of the facilities. It also lowered the combat-readiness of our soldiers, so we had every right to eliminate those provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So how did the whole of that situation resolve? How did it come to an end?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of September, these forces launched an attack on our facilities. I'm talking about Sibenik. So those forces used firearms and engaged in combat against us. On that particular day, fighting started all over Croatia, not only in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning of your testimony, you said that you were wounded, that you were injured. How did that and what was the outcome of your injury, and where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: When you asked me about my career, I said that, indeed. I said that I was injured in my command by a shell shrapnel. I still have two shrapnel in the brain because I was wounded in the head, in the shoulder, and in the knee. However, the situation was such that the ambulance, the medical organs of the Sibenik barracks crossed over to the other side. They were mostly Croatians, and they joined their people, so there was no way anybody could provide me with first aid. The then-chief of medical department of the 8th naval district took me to the hospital in Sibenik. I believe that he actually handed me over deliberately because he remained living in Sibenik after that. I was given an anti-tetanus shot there mand after that I was half conscious. Some ZNG members arrived and they took me to the Sibenik prison, to the district prison in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you here. We don't want to depart too far from the topic. I would kindly ask you to tell me whether you were exchanged, and where? Which unit did you join after that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I was exchanged on the 2nd of November, 1991, and that was the third exchange that took place. There were two exchanges before that, but I was not exchanged on those two occasions; it was only on the third occasion. Whenever the Red Cross came to the prison, they blindfolded me and took me out of my cell to some basement rooms. They were in fact hiding me because I hadn't been reported, but fortunately in the Knin corps they knew that I was there, and they insisted on having me brought for exchange, and they gave a major and 50 shoulders in exchange for me because you, yourself, are well aware that an exchange is a form of trade. After that, I went to Belgrade to the medical military academy to be medically examined because I had been tortured both physically and psychologically in prison. Every day they beat me up; they threw tear gas into my cell. After this, I was transferred to the Knin garrison, and I have already told you what duty I took up there. My immediate superior was Colonel Zdravko Tolimir when I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You've already answered my next question. I was going to ask you who your immediate superior was.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now that we are talking about this, it might be interesting to mention that naval Captain Beara was the superior of Colonel Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And where was Colonel Beara at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he was exactly, but the command of the naval military district was relocated to Kumbor, I believe, in Montenegro, and I think that's where the command of the naval military district was. We were not in contact at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After your exchange, when you were transferred to a new unit, the Knin corps, did you have any contacts with Captain Beara, Naval Captain Beara?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, because there was already fighting going on. It wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Mitrovic, when did you begin serving in the Army of Republika Srpska and in what unit?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I joined the Army of Republika Srpska on the 25th of May - if I'm not wrong - 1992, when I was transferred from Knin to the Drvar garrison and appointed chief of intelligence and security affairs of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At that time, was Colonel Beara in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: In that period, no, to the best of my knowledge. Why? Well, because he arrived later on, either at the end of 1992 or the beginning or the middle of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but tell me: How do you learn when Colonel Beara arrived in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I learned it either through a dispatch or through information sent around by the Main Staff telling us that the Naval Captain Beara had been appointed chief of security in the sector for intelligence and security affairs in the Main Staff, or perhaps we talked on the phone. I can't really be very precise about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the duty you were performing at the time, do you know what duty he was performing in that period?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I told you that he was appointed chief of the security administration, and I have to tell you that I was pleasantly surprised by his arrival because I knew that he was a professional, and I believed he was being appointed to the right post. I was surprised, also, because I considered him to be a Croat by ethnicity because he spoke like a Croat. He used the Latin alphabet when he was writing something. I associated him with a well known football player, the goalkeeper Beara from Split. However, later on I learned that he was a Serb and that he had been born in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mitrovic, what legal regulations and rules did you apply in the Army of Republika Srpska in your service?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: In the Army of Republika Srpska, the security organs like the entire army took over the rules of the then-JNA. In particular, in our service these were the rules of service of the security organ, the instruction on applying the methods and means of work, the rules of service of the military police, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could we now have in e-court document P407. We have an ERN number in the B/C/S version, 00909825; and in English, it's 00920108. Mr. Mitrovic, I'll ask you to take a look at item 16, 17, and 18 here. As you can see, we saw the first document telling us that these were the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And this is the chapter dealing with management of security organs. Please look at the three paragraphs I mentioned, and tell me when you are ready.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I can answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Based on these regulations, please tell me: What was the system of management of security organs in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, these paragraphs of these rules regulate precisely the manner in which security organs are managed. In paragraph 16, it says that the security organ is directly subordinate to the commanding officer of the command unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces in whose strength it is placed in the establishment. That is the gist of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, let's be specific about this. In your situation in the 2nd Krajina Corp., bearing in mind the duty you were performing, to whom were you directly subordinate?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: To my corps commander. [Realtime transcript read in error, "co-commander"]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And bearing in mind these rules, does that mean that in the entire organisation of the Army of Republika Srpska, these rules had to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It says here in all units, institutions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes -- one moment Mr. Nikolic. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to enter a correction into the transcript. Page 13, line 4, the witness said, to my commander, "my corps commander."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back for a minute to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To whom were you subordinate in the 2nd Krajina corps?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: To the commander of my corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the security -- or rather, were the security organs independent in their actions under these rules?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. Security organs cannot be independent because, first of all, they are accountable to their commander; secondly, they are accountable to their superior officer from the security service, so what sort of independence could there be? And they have to adhere to the law and to the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the provisions you've just looked at, tell me: What was the relationship between the subordinate and superior security organs in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was a vertical relationship, and it referred only to professional guidance of the security organ. This was done by superiors for their subordinates, but this was only professional guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about this. What do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, first of all, when we are talking about this I'm referring to counterintelligence, primarily, and the application of the methods of work of the security organ and the means of work. The superior security organ, they were always more experienced and better-qualified officers who were able to have an overview of the problem and provide guidance to their subordinate organ as to how this problem could be solved in the field of counterintelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 17, and tell me: What were the powers of the security organ as regards applying the methods and means of work?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: This paragraph deals in detail with the methods and means, and it refers to the legality of work. As regards applying the methods and means of work, it's the federal secretary who corresponded to ministerial rank. He was a minister in the old system, and he would authorize the army commander, and in peacetime it was the commander of the army who was the highest ranking, the ultimate authority who was familiar with the work of the security organ, and when there was combined applications of methods and means of work, he knew about it, and he also approved a secret means and methods of work. In wartime it would be the corps commander who would do all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I now wish to put a few questions to you about the security organ and the military police. What regulations did you use, if any, in performing your duties as regards the relationship between the security organ and the military police? And before you reply, I'll ask to have in e-court Document -- the same document but page 00909826 in B/C/S, and in English, 00920109. That's page 18 in B/C/S and page 11 in English. Can you see it, Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please be kind enough to tell us what paragraph 23 provides for.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you first asked me what rules we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: We used the rules of service of the military police that had been taken over, and this relationship was regulated by law, and the rules of service of the security service also deal with this. Paragraph 23 days that the security organ of a commanding unit institution and so on provides a specialist or professional management for a military police unit, and he is responsible for the unit being well equipped, ready for action, and so on and so forth, and the commander of the unit within whose composition the unit is -- let me clarify. If, for example, there is a military police battalion in the corps, which was the case where I was, I would propose to the commander how the battalion could be used, and he could accept or reject my proposal, but he issued orders to the commander of the battalion of the military police directly, and this is provided for in this rule. The military police units are subordinate to the commander of the unit they form a part of. So, for example, the commander of the brigade or the -- in the case of a battalion to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 23, the paragraph 3 thereof, starting with the words "the engagement of units" or "the deployment of units" or "individual members." Could you please look at that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I've had a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you paraphrase this paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: This is exactly about what I've just been talking about. I send my proposal to the commander, and the commander then either approves or disproves the use of military police unit, i.e., the deployment of the military police unit. That's how I understand this paragraph, and this has to be done with the consent of the superior military officer. In my case, I had to have the approval of the corps commander, i.e., his consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will no longer need this document, and we will proceed, moving to something else. Mr. Mitrovic, during that period of time from the moment you learned that Mr. Beara was, again, the security organ, did you and how often had contacts with him, and I mean professional contacts.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Of course we had contacts. We had face-to-face contacts, we contacted by phone, by telegrams, by official correspondence, and so on and so forth. Captain Beara was conscientious person, and in -- subject to his other commitments and plans he would come to the corps zone four or five times, and then that's when we would see each other. And there were also cases when he summoned him to come to Banja Luka, for example, if he was there to report to him there. It all depended on the current combat situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So when we are talking about the arrivals of your superior officer and when we talk about professional management, what did the rules prescribe and how things looked in practice when Colonel Beara arrived in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina corps?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Look, when he arrived in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina corps, Naval Captain Beara would first pay a visit to the corps commander. This is a custom, isn't it; when you visit somebody's house, you first say hello to the host. And then naval captain would brief the corps commander and inform him about his plan of the tour of the security organ and the aim of the inspection. He would inspect the departments in the corps and the security departments in the brigades during his visits. Only after that would a naval captain come to the offices of the security department, and there we would report to him. We would brief him on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of these official visits, could you give us an illustration, an example when Colonel Beara insisted on a different application of rules?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Of course not. Absolutely not. He was the beacon of the protection of legality. Actually, it would first be the commander and then everybody else down the ranks. So he was the one who made sure that the legality of the rules was respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the military police. I would like to show you Document number P707 in B/C/S; ERN number is 02072110. And in the English version, the ERN is 03041648. In B/C/S, page 32, and in English, it is page 22. Mr. Mitrovic, tell me, please, briefly, what are the duties and tasks of the military police, just in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I would say tasks rather than duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: These tasks are defined by the rules of service of the military police; and first and foremost, they mean that -- providing security of -- for facilities, commanders, other persons, routes, roads, and one of the priority purposes of the military police units was to fight infiltrated sabotage and terrorist groups. Within the scope of their work, the police had various services; and when we talk about services, I'd like to say that those services were the security service, the duty service, the patrol service, the escort service, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can the document be lowered? Can we scroll down and display Item number 55, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, let's look at Item 55 where one of the military police duties is mentioned, and that is escort service.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I've had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me briefly: What would be the tasks prescribed by the rules of service of the military police according to this item?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to escort service, this item defines the categories of persons which may be escorted by the military service; and primarily, these are persons who have been apprehended for having committed a crime and so on and so forth, and this is basically the long and the short of it. These persons would be escorted to a military prison or to another type of detention facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Have you read the Item 55 to the end? Did the military police have any powers or authorities in terms of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Military police had powers and the authority to escort prisoners of war from their temporary detention units at the brigade level to the prisoner of war camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll no longer need this document. And now, when we are talking about the relationship between the security organ and the military police, you have already stated that your relationship towards the military police was primarily in professional terms. Could you please be more specific? Could you please provide us with some more details and explain this term "professional terms," the essence of the term; what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: My obligation was to primarily make sure that the military police unit is manned by professionals or if there are no such men that there was training to provide professional education. In war there were very few professionals, so there were a lot of training courses organised for those who joined. The second task would be to control the training levels of the military police unit and its capabilities, and it was done during the war whenever possible. The next task would be to make sure that the military police units were equipped with all the means that were necessary for the performance of the unit's task, starting with flak jackets, APCs, and other very specific pieces of equipment, technical equipment and material that are indispensable for the work of a military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It arises from your answer that during the war you did not have enough professionals to work in the military police. How did you resolve that? How did you deal with that situation?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, there was a hovering problem of professionals not only in the military police but also in the security organs because there was a lack of professional servicemen, especially in the military police units. There were not enough men -- and I apologise for speeding. There were not enough men who had completed the appropriate training courses in the intelligence and security training centre in Pancevo. That's why we had to make do with what we had. If somebody -- a certain profile -- professional was necessary, we either had him or not, but that was not just the case in the military police, but there was also problem with the brigade commands. For example, in the brigade commands there would be, perhaps, one or two professionals, and the others had been recruited from the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, let's go back to your contacts with Mr. Beara, who was your superior at the time. What was your attitude towards the problems that you have just shared with us? Was he aware of such problems? Did you brief him about the problems that you faced?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Of course I briefed my superior about the situation in the military police unit, and I also asked for his assistance, both with the equipping of the units as well as with the professional staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And did you receive any assistance, and how was the assistance provided to you?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: There was assistance. For example, if there were men in another unit of a different corps, for example, Bosnia or Herzegovina corps, and if they had a surplus of such men, then they would be re-assigned to come and work with -- in my corps. They had broader possibilities than I did, and the same applied to the equipment that I mentioned. The security administration is in charge of making sure that the units of the military police were well equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You have stated that your professional contacts took place in various shapes and forms; either Mr. Beara would come to the zone of responsibility of the 2nd corps or you would go and meet him somewhere else. Did Mr. Beara arrive in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina corps in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Naval Captain Beara did come to the zone of responsibility of the corps. At that time it was either in mid-July or in the second half of the month of July; I'm not sure. I remember the instance very well because it was a few days prior to the fall of Glamoc and Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When was that? When did that line fall?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Grahovo fell into the hands of the enemy on the 27th of July and Glamoc on the 28th of July. So that is some -- there is one event that I tie to his arrival, and the second event was the fact that I took the opportunity given the dire situation in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps in the face of the attacks of the Croatian army on the one hand and the Muslim army on the other hand, and we also were exposed to the HVO attacks. In other words, the situation on the frontline was rather difficult. And in the meantime, I had introduced upon the approval of the corps commander the measures against a person from the corps command, operative measures to be very precise, and that person had provided confidential data to an unauthorized person, and that is why operative measures were introduced against that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we please just briefly go into closed session because I'm going to mention some names that should not be mentioned in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to tell you that towards the end of 1994 and the beginning of 1995 was a very difficult period. During that period, there was a lot of antagonism between MUP members and the military members, and that antagonism had been created by the then-politics of the SDS. Because of this antagonism and conflicts, the normal flow of information had been interrupted between the intelligence and security organs and the MUP organs. You know, the rule was that information would flow vertically from me, or if you start with the corps brigade security administration and then added the level of the administration for security, the exchange of information would be carried out. While the relationship was good, we at lower levels could also be involved in the exchange of information with our peer services, which is normally provided for by the rules of service of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P407 in e-court, please. In the B/C/S version, it's number 00909828; and in English, it's 00920112. Mr. Mitrovic, I'll ask you to look at paragraph 31 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, can this be moved? Yes, thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, now you've seen it and read it. Was this the basis on which your measures were taken?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was the basis in wartime. You must bear in mind that it was war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And who did you inform of this?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, first I reported to the commander and the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When reporting to your commander on the introduction of these measures, was Colonel Beara present?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, first I must emphasize that operative processing was introduced before the arrival of Naval Captain Beara sometime in late May or in June, and this processing was being done. We asked for the application of secret methods, and this was approved by the corps commander because under the instructions on the methods -- implementation of the methods and means of work, he is the authorised superior officer mentioned in paragraph 17. And as the situation at the front was very difficult, I took this opportunity to inform Naval Captain Beara of the overview of our work, and I asked him for guidance as to what should be done next, first of all, because the situation at the frontline was very difficult and we didn't have much time to deal with these -- or rather, with this officer. So we agreed to put him under control until the end of the offensive and then to put a stop to this activity, which is what we did sometime in September of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need this document anymore. I'll put my next question. Within the scope of these activities, was it your duty to regularly inform Colonel Beara for this.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On what basis?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was my superior along the professional line, and this was a counterintelligence problem and, of course, I had to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the course of this conversation, you mentioned that the background of this whole case was a conflict between the Ministry of the Interior and the Army of Republika Srpska concerning the exchange of important information. My question is as follows: How was the flow of information regulated in that period?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, according to the rules of service of the security organ, there is a chapter there dealing with relations with similar services, services which are akin: the MUP, the state security, and so on and so forth. So this wasn't optional. It wasn't a discretionary matter. So it was the security administration or the security sector for intelligence and security which exchanged information at the level of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. At corps level, exchange of information was conducted with public security centres and at brigade level with local public security stations. That's how it was regulated in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And what in particular was the conflict about? Why did this break out?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was because of these false reports sent by individual members of the state security - I won't say that they were all doing this - and also some members of the MUP, reports concerning the situation at the frontline. I told their chiefs, please, feel free to come and ask for whatever information you are interested in; there's no reason for you to illegally visit the units, and this did occur, and then send reports which are not true, and then the officers are blamed. At the same time, individual members of the MUP said they didn't need officers, that they were educated to command brigades and other units. These were people who had completed reserve officer training many years ago, and now they thought they were able to command the corps, I ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, this conflict, was it ever resolved, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: This activity was interrupted with the arrest of this person we mentioned, and the filing of a criminal report and the submission of this whole case to the military investigation organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And please tell me, when did this happen? When was this conflict concerning the exchange of information between these services which are akin resolved, and when was the legal framework restored?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe I'm subjective, but this situation obtained until the end of the war. There were even situations where we were engaged in combat together, and the separate MUP staff would be established, for example, in Petrovci, and the corps command would be in Ostrelj, so regardless of the fact that the MUP units were being used in the theatre of war, which was the responsibility of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, very briefly, please tell me: In addition to your testimony today, did you ever have an interview with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 2004 -- I think it was in June, in 2004 when I was interviewed by an investigator of this Tribunal. The interview lasted for two days. I can give you names if need be. I had the status of suspect in the case against Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could I check my notes, please. Would it be convenient to take a break now, and then I'll be very brief after the break and round off my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Nikolic. We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you. --- Break taken at 3.39 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic -- Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It won't take long now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, let's try and clarify one thing. When I asked you about the arrival of Mr. Beara in the territory of the 2nd Krajina Corps, could you be more specific and tell us: When did he arrive, bearing in mine the objective events such as the fall of the Glamoc and Grahovo line?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: The most specific thing that I can tell you is that it was a few days before the fall of Grahovo and Glamoc. I remember that well for two reasons as I've told you, but I wouldn't be able to give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And just one more thing: Do you remember, how much time did Colonel Beara spend in the territory?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Given the situation on the frontline, he stayed at the corps command for just one day or several hours, not longer. He did not have much time, and then he proceeded according to plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. President I have no further questions for this witness. I would just like to add one more thing. At one point we were in private session, and as I looked at the transcript we are of the opinion that not everything has to be in private session from page 22, line 24, to page 23, line 12. This is the part that don't have to be in private session because they don't contain any elements that would call for a private session. At least that's our opinion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree to that, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any of the other parties, judges? All right. Okay. So that part that you have indicated, Madam Registrar would have certainly taken note of which pages and lines will no longer remain in private session. Yes. Mr. Zivanovic, do you have a cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have already met, but I will introduce myself for the record. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and I represent Vujadin Popovic in this case. I would like to ask you, first of all, whether you know Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us since when have you known him, and how did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know Mr. Vujadin Popovic, and I met him in Drvar when I first took the position that I have already spoken about, and for a while Vujadin Popovic was a desk officer in the department for security and intelligence of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, at the time you were his immediate superior; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately, how long did he remain working in the same department as you and where you were his superior?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: After my arrival in May 1992, he stayed until the moment the Drina Corps was established. At that moment, upon my proposal, given that the be fact that he was a promising officer at the time who was captain 1st class, Mr. Popovic was re-assigned to the Drina Corps in order to take up the position of the chief of the intelligence and security department in that corps because he hails from Vlasenici. That was one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While he worked in your department, in the security department in Drvar, what was your impression of his professional qualities and personal qualities that he displayed during his work?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that at the time Mr. Popovic was captain 1st class. He was a very responsible officer, very conscientious. Whatever tasks he was entrusted with, he performed well in time and professionally correct. When I speak about him as a person, I have to say that he was -- he had a very good sense of humour. He liked to sing and play instruments. Everybody liked him. However, he was a professional, a very promising officer, and that's why I recommended him for promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were positioned in the 2nd Krajina Corps, were there any members of other ethnic groups in the 2nd Krajina Corps, i.e., people who were non-Serbs or non-Montenegrins?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were quite a few such persons or individuals. For example, the commander of the command office was a Muslim officer. I can share his name with you if that would be of some significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we can go into private session if that is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to go into private session, please decide, Mr. Zivanovic, and I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If we could, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that straightaway. I think it will simplify matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We are in open session, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I wanted to ask you this: What was the attitude of Vujadin Popovic towards these corps members who were of a different ethnic group? Did you notice anything unusual? Did you glean any intolerance towards members of others in the groups while you were his superior?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see any such thing. There was no intolerance, nor did I expect Popovic to display any sign of intolerance because it's simply not the person that he is. He was a JNA officer, and it was only normal that we had people from all over the place in our midst. In our units, there were people from all over Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that attitude remained unchanged while he was a member of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there were people of other ethnic groups in your unit, could you tell us whether that remained the fact until the end of the war, or was it only of one particular period?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: These people remained on the strength of the corps until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try and complete my examination within the 15 minutes that I asked for, but I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to grant me a possible extension of maybe 10 minutes or 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Nikolic, your team has been extremely cooperative, so please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Jelena Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I represent Mr. Drago Nikolic in this case. I would like to ask you something about the topics that you've already told us something about during your testimony today. It arises from your testimony that you spent your entire career working in the security organs?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You have a very rich experience when it comes to the application of the rules of service of the security organs and working in security organs?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Judging from your testimony, the Army of Republika Srpska after the year 1992 fully adopted and implemented the rules of security organs and other rules from the previous JNA; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, in the course of 1994 and 1995, a document was issued under the title "The Instruction Of the Main Staff." The number is P2741 in e-court, 2741, and this instruction regulates the issues of command and control of the security organ. Mr. Mitrovic, could you please look at that document. You will find the B/C/S version on the right-hand side of the screen. As the chief of security of the 2nd Krajina Corps, did you have an occasion to see this document in the course of 1995? Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: This document was indeed issued in 1994 and now -- as I'm reading this instruction now, I remember it. I know what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please pay attention to the first paragraph starting with the words: "Lately, frequent problems, failures, and irregularities have been registered in command and control over the security organ." And this instruction refers to these problems as the rationale for issuing this instruction. Do you know what problems and irregularities turned up in the command and control of the security organs in the Army of Republika Srpska in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in the preamble the reason is given why these instructions had to be compiled and sent to the lower-ranking units. There were irregularities in the manner in which command and control was exercised by individual commanders at various levels in relation to the security organs. All I know is that the commanders often sent security organs to perform tasks which were not part of their prescribed duties. In the course of the war, the commander would often go and tell me to bring back a unit from its position or to try and prevent people running away from their positions or to go and disarm paramilitary units if they turned up, and they did, in the zone of the corps, and so on and so forth, and this was not our domain of work. Also, there were certain commanders who designated security organs to be on duty in the commands even though it was well known that their stints of duty were to be within the security organ, not outside it. Further, there were commanders who opened mail even though they were not authorised to do so, mail sent to the security organs. There were such things happening, and all this indicated that there were irregularities in command and control in relation to the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify why the commanders had limitations when it comes to opening mail sent to the security organs in the units in which the security organs were active?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, first of all, it's not polite to open somebody else's mail - that's the first point - because every document received by the security organ was always sent to him personally. It wasn't sent to the commander. Why they did this, well, you should probably ask them, but they were not authorised to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And the correspondence, or rather, the communication that went along the professional line of the security organs, did it contain details from the counterintelligence work or other forms of work of the security organs?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Most often, these were counterintelligence issues and also overall security, so the issues in question were such that only the corps commander would be informed of them. Not brigade commanders, for example, but I can clarify if you like. There are certain situations where a brigade commander would be informed by the security organ of certain cases from the counterintelligence assessment. This information reflected the situation in the unit, in the area of responsibility, and so on, and they could know about this. But what was secret from the level of the brigade commander, and this was prescribed by the rules, was the application of secret methods of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Rule 153 in the methods of work?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's defined in the instructions, yes. The secret methods are defined there and those that are not secret.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I now wish to show you another document. Could we have in e-court 7D576. This is a document not from your unit, 17D176. I do apologise; the number in the transcript is wrong. 7DP176. Thank you. This is a document which was not issued by your corps, but it illustrates precisely what you have just described. Would you please look at the title. It says: "Warning Regarding Prevention of Leaking of Secret Information." Please read this document silently to yourself just to see what it's about, and then I will put two or three questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: According to your many years of experience as chief of the security organ, does this document show that all persons who come into contact with secret information are duty-bound to give a written declaration and to keep secret the information they have gleaned from unauthorized opening of mail sent to the security organ?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, you can see that the brigade commander opened mail addressed to the security organ, although he was not authorised to do so, and according to the normal procedure he was supposed to sign a written declaration stating that he would keep confidential the information he had learned in this manner. There were instances where people opened mail sent to the security organ by accident, and then they would sign the declaration. This was the procedure to be followed according to the rules. Security organs also have to sign a declaration that they will keep information confidential when they are leaving the service, for example, or retiring, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Look at point 6 of this document, item 6. You have explained to us what the procedure was. My question is the following: Can this letter or this warning be considered to be a disciplinary measure or a threat to the commander?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, by no means. It is only a warning asking him not to do this again.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the document we discussed previously. Could we have again P2741 in e-court, please, page 1, item 2, second paragraph. In item 2, second paragraph, can we have the B/C/S version. Can we scroll the B/C/S version, yes, so that Mr. Mitrovic can see it. In paragraph 2, it says that all members of these organs and services are authorised by law to act and work on tasks from their field of work analogous to the authority of the members of the RS MUPs, state security department. Could you please tell us what this means, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: What this in fact means is that we perform the tasks of state security in the army - that's the simplest explanation - and we are authorised to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on your years of experience, Mr. Mitrovic, can you tell us -- you were the security organs. If a security organ violated the rules or the law, the commander of the unit he is in, does he have the right to initiate procedure to have this chief of security replaced?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, because he is his immediate superior. Regardless of the fact that he is a security organ, if he violates discipline or commits a crime, he is not amnestied.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, who monitors the professionalism and lawfulness of the work of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Monitoring of professionalism and lawfulness is carried out by the superior in the security organ who monitors his subordinate organs. That's the basic principle. And by your leave, I'd like to add in relation to what you asked me just before, the commander does have the right to ask for the dismissal, the replacement of the security organ. There was a situation, for example, in the Kupres brigade where the security chief and the commander fell in love with the same woman, and their mutual cooperation and relations became impossible, and the commander asked for the security organ to be transferred from his unit. He asked this of the corps commander, of course, and we did this so that normal relations could be re-established.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When answering this question regarding the monitoring of professionalism and lawfulness in the work of the security organ, as we laypersons are a bit confused by this description, 80 percent and 20 percent of security and staff work respectively, so does the commander's authority, or rather, the monitoring extend to the 20 percent, or is it somebody else who does that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: This figure in my view is there to tell commanders that security organs should have time to do their work. I'm referring primarily to counterintelligence activity, and this is normal in wartime. It's quite normal, but how much 80 percent is, well, there are no working hours in wartime. You work day and night. You are up at all hours, so it's very hard to define this precisely. The idea was to let the commanders know that they should allow these people to do their work and give them fewer tasks of other kinds. You asked about the 20 percent. Well, if these are staff security tasks you would do that in the command, and of course, the commander and all the members of the command can see what you are doing, and they know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In case of criminal or legal activities, police actions, who oversees the work of the organ?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if we are talking about the -- I apologise to the interpreters. I apologise to the Court. All those jobs that you referred to are in the security organ's domain of work, and this is, again, something that is done immediately by the security organ's superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I just want to go back to a question that I put slightly earlier. I asked you, in the case that the security organ violates a law or initiates a security measure, can the chief [as interpreted] initiate measures against his security organ by bringing this problem up before the superior command, let's say, from the corps to the staff or from the brigade to the corps?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My colleague has just warned me that we have in the transcript on page 40, line 9, I think that the question was: "Can the commander initiate measures..." and in the transcript it says "chief." So can we just correct this? Perhaps we can listen to it again and have it corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can I reply? The commander can initiate even the replacement of the security organ if he is not satisfied with his work, and he does that. For example, if it's me, the corps commander can initiate this replacement towards the commander of the Main Staff or towards the chief of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Chairman. Yes, Judge, we do have questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were talking about the relationships existing between you and the security organ in the staff. Is it true that there were the exchange information between your organ in the 2nd corps and the organ in the Main Staff responsible for security and counterintelligence?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you the document. This is Document 5D1192. This is a document coming from the security and -- sector of the staff, of the Main Staff. Can we see the second page of this document. You can see at the bottom of this document, we can see that this document bears the name of Zdravko Tolimir, and right below we can see that it was sent to the security and intelligence department of the 1st Krajina Corps, the 2nd Krajina Corps, and the other corps of the Republika Srpska. Can you confirm that this document had actually been sent to your organ and your corps?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Most probably it was because in this dispatch you can see that it's going to the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I now would like to know -- we can go back to page 1 of this document, but before we look at this document, can you tell me whether you had the information concerning smuggling in of weapons or oil in humanitarian assistance?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did some -- have some indications of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And I would like to read the first paragraph and the beginning of the second paragraph of this document. In this document, it is stated: [In English] "With the help of international organisations, allies in the west, and Islamic countries, the Muslims are continuing intensively to import weapons, ammunition, and military equipment via Croatian territory. Under the guise of sending family packages, around 400 parcels, on 29 May a convoy was sent from Austria with ammunition and military equipment for use by the 2nd corps of the so-called BH Army. The transport has been organised by a certain Norwegian member of UNHCR called Mak. We have also noted that UNPROFOR is supplying the so-called BH Army." [Interpretation] Before we move on to another question, can you confirm that your corps, the 2nd corps of the army in Bosnia, can you confirm that your corps was actually -- had something to do with the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the information mentioned here, because here we're talking about the 2nd corps of the army, the BH Army, but did you have similar information concerning the corps of the Bosnia or Herzegovina army which was in the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did have some indications that supplies were being provided by land and air to the 5th corps of the B&H army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you a document. This is Document 5D1195. This is a document from the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 5th corps. You can see that at the top of the document. Is it correct to say that the 5th corps was based in the Bihac pocket? We are talking about the 5th corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We can read right below the name of the person who wrote the document. We see what it's talking about, and we see that this is a logistics report concerning the receipt of a shipment by UNHCR, and there is an acronym, UBS. Can you tell me what "UBS" means?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: This is the usual abbreviation for devices for killing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... items sent out and indicated in this document, we realise that we are talking about weapons here, right? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I now would like to show you another document, 5D1196. This is a document coming from the Bosnia-Herzegovina embassy in Croatia, which was sent out to the 5th corps. Do you agree with that, the 5th corps of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And here, again, we can see that the items mentioned here are weapons, actually?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And right at the bottom of this page, can we see the bottom of the page in English? Actually, it's the second page in the English version. Excuse me. So right at the bottom of this page in the B/C/S version, we can see that the truck bears the number UNHCR 10379. From the information you had in your job, did you ever hear that the UNHCR is -- that this organisation transported these weapons and was responsible for smuggling weapons or oil?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were indications of that. Specifically, I heard that the ammunition was packed in sardine cans and so on. I said that this was also done by air; things were dropped by a parachute in wooden crates. This is how ammunition and other equipment was delivered.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked not to overlap. MADAM FAUVEAU: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... 97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, in fact you were overlapping. If you could together with the witness please try to avoid it as much as you can. Even though you are not speaking the same language, still, it's a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now show the witness Document 5D1197. Earlier on, you told us that you did have indications about smuggling, weapon-smuggling. This is another document from the Embassy of the Republic of the BH in the Republic of Croatia as sent to the 5th corps, and in this document we can see that -- at the very beginning of this document we can read: [In English] "The Bihac district office has sent 70 tonnes of D-2 fuel from the 5th corps from the ARBH Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina fuel contingent. Transport is carried out by UNHCR." [Interpretation] Did you also get some information about fuel-smuggling?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: We did have indications that this was also done with oil, and you know that fuel is a strategic material or asset in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My colleague reminded you that you had an interview with the -- in the Prosecutor's Office in 2004, and I would like to read you an excerpt from this interview. It's Document 5D1193, page 83. In this interview, amongst other things you mentioned the signature on the military documents. You explained who signs these document, who has the authority to sign these documents, and how they are signed. And you said: [In English] "You can sign, you know, the everyday report, everyday documents, combat reports, and staff. You can sign that for someone. But if these documents were more important, if you were talking about operations, about directives, about orders for the attack or defence, then, you know, the Commander couldn't be absent. So he would then sign himself." [Interpretation] Based on what you said, could we conclude that all documents are not as important as the daily -- the everyday documents sent from one unit to the others are not necessarily as important as orders concerning a specific operation?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Depending on what I said on that interview and based on what you've said, daily reports, combat readiness that was -- that were dispatched, if -- or for example, the daily report sent from my organ to the security administration if I was absent, this report could be signed by my deputy. But what you asked about documents, orders to execute some kind of combat assignment or an operation, defence operation or an attack, equally, then the person had to be the commander in this case. He could not be absent from the unit while his unit was getting ready to go off into battle or preparing to execute an operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I have another question for you. Did you have any information -- or do you know whether President Karadzic sometimes gave orders directly to the corps without going through the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm familiar with such situations. I will give you an example, when Karadzic ordered General Talic to begin the Prsten, ring, operation in the Posavina, and the Main Staff was not informed about the operation and that it would begin. I remember that because my corps at that time was denied the ammunition that was essential to us, which Talic took for himself and used in that operation ring, Prsten. There were also -- there was also talk that General [as interpreted] Karadzic was issuing orders to General Milosevic in the Sarajevo-Romanija corps. Yeah, there were examples. MADAM FAUVEAU: [Interpretation] I believe there's a mistake in the transcript. On page 12 [as interpreted] we can read "General Karadzic," but I don't believe that the witness stated that. He only said Karadzic, I believe, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about page 46, line 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Mr. Mitrovic, my name is Dragan Krgovic. On behalf of the Defence team, I'm going to ask you a few questions about some things that you've already spoken about today. Mr. Mitrovic, you have spoken at great length about the work of your organ and the way things functioned in your corps.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If I ask you about the Main Staff and the relationship between certain people in the Main Staff and how they exchange information, you could only answer by assumptions?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I agree because I never worked in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krgovic please come closer to the microphone. It's practically impossible to hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, we have the same problem as yesterday. I don't know how I can help you more than mentioning it. You need to come closer to the microphone, please. Thank you. The microphone can't come up any further. No, it's fixed. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, what you have spoken about today mostly concerns the principles of work in the corps and its subordinated units, especially in your corps?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this. In answering my friend Nikolic's questions, you have also spoken about combat activities in the summer of 1995 in the western part of the frontline in the zone of responsibility of your corps.
