Do you remember when combat was launched, i.e., when the Muslim-Croat forces launched their attack in the zone of responsibility of your corps?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you the precise date. I know that the preparations started sometime towards the end of July -- June, and if we're talking about the Glamoc axis, members of the Croatian army took Mali Sator feature, which is the most dominant feature near Glamoc. As of the end of June, the intercity of the operations stepped -- was stepped up for the rest of the month and culminated with the fall of the part of the territory that we have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Given the critical situation in the zone of responsibility, did officers of the Main Staff arrive in the zone of responsibility of your corps in the period leading up to the fall of Glamoc and around the fall of Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the Main Staff did come to the zone of responsibility, and I can even give you their names if you want me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I'll give you those that I can remember. There was General Jovica Maric, who hails from Glamoc, so he had some personal interest in the territory. There was also General Tolimir who was there for awhile. He hails from Glamoc. General Gvero also came. He hails from Mrkonic Grad. General Zivorad Ninkovic, also from Glamoc, also came; and General Milovanovic was at the forward command post of the Main Staff, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, I am interested in a very concrete issue. During the time surrounding the fall of Glamoc and Grahovo, did you see General Gvero in the zone of responsibility of your corps?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I saw General Gvero around the fall of Glamoc; to be more precise, on the 28th of July. He arrived together with General Jovica Maric. Why do I remember this? The Croatian air force was opening fire on our positions around that time, and they attacked with chemical weapons, and there were dozens of members of the Glamoc brigade who suffered the effects of the chemical weapons that the Croats used. The two generals, Maric, who was the chief of the air force in the Main Staff, and General Gvero to raise the morale of the fighters and the people had who had been chased from their homes arrived in the zone of responsibility of our corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the position of General Maric because it hasn't been recorded properly in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the air force of the Army Republika Srpska in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. I believe that was the official title of his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please repeat the date when you saw the two generals?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That was the day when Glamoc fell?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's when the enemy forces entered Glamoc and when our units left Glamoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise; did you say that in your previous answer, as well, because it wasn't recorded properly the first time around.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit 6D306.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a translation of the original, which is in English. We have the sufficient number of photocopies of our draft translation. I would kindly ask the usher to distribute these among the Prosecutor, the Trial Chamber. The official translation is still pending.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter apologises. The original is in B/C/S, and the translation is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mitrovic, this is a document which you sent to the Main Staff in December 1995. Does this document describe the event that you have just spoken about?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my report, i.e., a report of the security organ describing precisely the events that I have just described, i.e., the chemical agents that were used on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the time of day when you saw General Gvero on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was during the day, while it was still light, but I can't tell you exactly when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, we are talking about two different dates. On the 27th of July, chemical agents were used; and then on the following day, you saw General Gvero on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the following day when the enemy forces entered Glamoc and when our units together with the civilian population left Glamoc, on the 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And where did you encounter General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was in the village of Kovacevici, after Glamoc, on the road from Glamoc towards Mlinista and Baraci. This is where the command of the third Serbian brigade was, at least for awhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the car that General Gvero arrived in, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. I don't. I suppose that he arrived in a Jeep or something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, at that time in July 1995, how long would it take to travel distance from Banja Luka to Han Pijesak by car?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Again, I could only give you my assumption or my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you were to take that journey from Banja Luka to Han Pijesak, how long would it have taken you at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I did the journey just once during the war. I was in our Main Staff only once, and I believe that it would have taken about eight hours approximately. I really don't know. It's very difficult for me to say because -- well, I can't be any more precise because the roads at that time were different than they are now. Things have changed. The intensity of the traffic was not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And from Banja Luka to Ostrelj, how long would it take?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: From Banja Luka to Ostrelj, about two to two and a half hours, approximately, and Mlinista is a bit further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where General Gvero left after this event, if you know, of course? Did anybody tell you anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that General Gvero went in the direction of Mlinista and Baraci because that's where the OG was and those were the next positions of the Army Republika Srpska after the fall of Glamoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just a few question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, when you were chief of security at the corps level, did you have a deputy?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I did have a deputy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you have other people who were subordinate to you, who answered to you?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: In the security department, I had subordinated desk officers who answered to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to speak to any of your subordinated officers about the way in which they were doing their job?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Every day. We analysed our work every day. Every day, we had meetings to discuss our further steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if you ever considered that one of your subordinated officers wasn't doing his job properly, did you have him into your office to speak to him about that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if you thought he was not doing his job properly, did you warn him about the performance of his job and how he was to do it in the future?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We would have a conversation, and I would warn him about things, and I would provide him with my remarks about his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would you not regard that as being a way of disciplining that officer?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. A disciplinary procedure is something that is provided for by the rules and regulations of service in the JNA, and these rules envisage disciplinary measures, and what you are talking about and what I'm talking about would have been just a conversation during which the officer would receive caution of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I see. Did you ever have occasion in which you had to decide whether one of your subordinated officers had broken the law or not?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any such situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But would you agree that another way of describing having to decide whether somebody has broken the law or not is monitoring the legality of their work?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I would agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would you also agree that if somebody has the exclusive right to do something, it means they are the only person who is permitted to do it?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I am afraid I don't know what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, what do you understand by the word "exclusive"?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I use the word myself when I spoke about the command in and control over security organs, and I said that unit commanders were exclusively superior to the security organs in their own units, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we'll move on. You've probably answered the question in a roundabout way. Just one other thing. During the course of your work, did you ever use human sources of intelligence, sometimes called "informants"?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: It is the obligation of the security organ to create collaborators with the security service, so the answer is, yes, I did. But these are not people to whom a derogatory term should be applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I didn't intend to apply a derogatory term to them if that's how it sounded through translation, but were some of these collaborators encouraged to give information by being given money?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: There were different motives out of which people agreed to cooperate with the security organs ranging from patriotism to money, as you say. The motive's different from one person to another, depending on the character and the significance of the person for the security organs. To put it more precisely, whether that person had access to information or not, that's what we were concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So were you involved in your service in paying money to informants, cash?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, I was not involved in such a situation, but we might have paid the travel expenses of these informers if they had to travel to a certain place where the meeting or the contact would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So did your service keep an amount of cash somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: The service had a certain amount of money in cash for expenses. In peacetime this would be approved by the army commander, and this money for expenses was used for per diem payments to security organs if they had to travel and to cover operative expenses. If you, for example, invite a collaborator to lunch, you can't expect him to pay. You pay, and you have to justify the expense by a valid financial document, a bill or receipt or such like, or a cheque.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that the position in wartime?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: In wartime, I never had expense money. There was none available.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just one other thing. You told us about a love triangle between a brigade commander and his chief of security. Can you give us an example of a chief of security ever being sacked by a brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I did not have such an example in the 2nd Krajina Corps. A brigade commander cannot sack him, but he can suggest that this person should no longer perform duties in the security organ of the Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Yes, Mr. Thayer, there's still time before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My name is Nelson Thayer, and I'll be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During the war, Colonel, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: During the war, I was not a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So not a member of SDS or the radicals?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Never, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And before the war when you were in the JNA, you were a member of the communist party, the Communist Alliance of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that was the norm for JNA officers, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was the norm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber how common it was for a JNA officer not to have been a member of the communist party?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: There were such officers, but a small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think as you put it in your interview with the OTP back in 2004, that was simply the world you were living in at the time; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we've heard from you today testimony about the friction or conflict that developed between the army on the one hand and the state security services and MUP on the other, you said, towards the end, I think, of 1994, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during the war, sir, there was a conflict that developed between the leadership of the political parties, for example, the SDS and the Radical party, as well as the political leadership of the Republika Srpska on the one hand and members of the VRS on the other. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You are probably referring to September 1993 when you mentioned the SDS and the Radical party. That was when manipulation of part of the units of the Army of Republika Srpska in Banja Luka occurred. They were dissatisfied, and rightly so, with their personal situation at the time, and it later transpired that the aim of this whole action was an attack on some soldiers. However, the slogan was, let's fight against war profiteers, against people who grow rich, but in the end these soldiers arrested certain officers. It was a rebellion of sorts, an uprising of sorts in the Army of Republika Srpska. I don't know if that's what you were referring to when you put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, that's partially what I'm referring to. The conflict or friction, however you want to put it, between the political leadership of Republika Srpska on the one hand and the army of the Republika Srpska, in particular its JNA-trained officer corps, that continued after 1993; is that correct, sir, after the September 1993 incident that you described.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, yes. This antagonism or this conflict escalated towards the end of the war. I don't want to prejudge things, but on the one hand you had the army, which was quite impoverished and which was fighting every day, and on the other hand you had the civilian leadership, people who were in the then-ruling party who took advantage of the war to enrich themselves personally, and this situation went on throughout the war but especially in the period I mentioned. Of course, it was quite natural that there should be dissatisfaction and that a conflict should arise. It went so far that humanitarian aid which arrived, for example, from Serbia, was sold by these people. They were members of the SDS, to make it quite clear. They were representatives of municipal organs, so they were deputies in the assembly and so on. For a time, there was even a situation where members of the municipal leadership of the SDS could not be mobilised, and that gave rise to conflicts as well; or you had situations where Karadzic ordered that from every municipal SDS, five SDS members were to be designated, and they had to be taken into the state security service, regardless of the fact that they knew nothing about the work of the service. I'm just trying to illustrate, but there were many other situations which all led to a conflict. There was an assembly meeting, which I did not attend, where all this escalated into an open conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as the conflict intensified, and putting aside the war profiteering for a moment, the conflict had a significant political element to it, as well; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The political leadership or politicians in the VRS -- I'm sorry, in the Republika Srpska would refer to officers of the army as "commies" or "reds" or "the red guards"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I personally was called those names. I was called a commie. But I'll tell you something interesting: Some of these SDS leaders had previously been members. For example, Dragan Karadzic had been a member of the central committee of the communist party, and he was not called a commie, but I was, and I was just a rank and file member of the party. So that was absurd, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your experience, those types of terms were used quite liberally against members of the VRS; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: If you are referring to terms such as "commies," "red guards," "reds," that was the usual terminology they used, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in fact, Colonel, basically any former JNA officer could be the target of such abuse in your experience; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? Basically, it is correct, but there were officers who immediately became close to that party and those organs, and they were not targeted. But I was not among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your experience, sir, the security organs came in for particular abuse along those lines in terms of being branded or called "commies" and "reds" and "red guards" and such; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they among others. Karadzic even introduced the term "5th column" or "6th column." I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber why you think the security organs were singled out for that type of attitude on President Karadzic's behalf?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can say that one of the reasons, certainly, was that the security organs made efforts to prevent crime, to prevent smuggling and black marketeering, to prevent the unlawfulness of the work of those organs, which was evident. There was a situation where a security organ from the Sarajevo-Romanija corps arrested Krajisnik's brother as a criminal, and Krajisnik was a high-ranking official. On the other hand, he had Karadzic's approval to import fuel without paying taxes or duties, and they all had that, practically. Also, there was a situation when Sanski Most was about to fall in 1995. It was on the point of falling, and the-then president of the municipality - he was most likely an SDS president, as well - issued approval for electrical appliances practically looted from houses to be used, well, for the Defence of Republika Srpska. That's absurd. So what I'm trying to say is -- well, that's what I understood you to ask, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have understood me, Mr. Thayer. It's time to have the break. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Good evening to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions along this line, and then I'm going to move on to a different subject. In your experience, during this period in which the animosity that you felt directed from the political leadership of the Republika Srpska increased towards the army, did you understand that - again, putting war profiteering to the side - also to be as a result of the particularly high political leadership in the Republika Srpska's belief that the power of the security organs of the army, whether that power was real or perceived by President Karadzic, presented a threat to him and the high political leadership in the Republika Srpska? I understand that was a very long question. Please, take your time to think it through. If I need to rephrase it, I will, but please take your time in answering that question.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: From my point of view, I can tell you that we were never a threat to the political leadership of Republika Srpska, nor we ever considered being one at all. The complete military and the security organs had just one focus, and that was war, unlike some members of the political leadership. The problems were mounting, and they were never dealt with, and in addition to the problems that I've already spoken about, the problems also reflected in the supplying of the troops, which did not function at all, and in any normal state, in the state of war, this is a matter of the civilian authorities. In our case, our unit commanders had to find their own means to get ahold of food, ammunition, clothes. All I'm saying is that they spent most of their time thinking about dealing with the logistics problems and less thinking about combat. In other words, we were never a threat. We took measures against those members of the SDS, and I don't mean to speak in general terms because there were some very commendable people there who were engaged in crime, who deserted from the front lines, and we did that in our own respective zone of responsibility, and this at one point culminated. And there was another thing that needs to mentioned. Certain local warlords were against the army, and they were permanently making efforts to create their own little armies that would be under their command, just like the situation was at the very beginning of the war when the Territorial Defence units and MUP units were under their command. I'm really not privy any -- to indicia to the effect that we were a threat to them. We just wanted everybody to do their own job and to put an end to criminal activities. They also had the state security service and MUP organs under their control, and of course, they had the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just follow up on that, if I may, Colonel. I understand what you're telling the Trial Chamber in terms of where you were coming from, as it were, as a member of the security organs. My question is, did you ever understand based on what was being said from the Republika Srpska political leadership that they perceived that the security organs of the army presented a threat to their power? Whether or not that was your intent, like I said, whether it was real or perceived on the part of the political leadership, was it ever your understanding that that was also a component of this increasing friction?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I don't know whether they considered the security organs a threat, whether they were intimidated by them. I suppose that they were because we were the ones who tried to curb some activities, and as far as the leadership is concerned, I really don't know of any measures being taken against them. They were independent in every possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And despite the -- this friction in 1994 and 1995 and the cessation of horizontal communication between yourself, for example, and your counterpart in the state security service or the MUP, despite that horizontal sharing of information which you said stopped at a particular time, it's the case that vertically, at the very top, there was communication between General Tolimir and Dragan Kijac, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Most probably. That's how things should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I believe as you told the investigators in Banja Luka in 2004, that information that they shared, if the VRS deemed it worthy, would then get transmitted to President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. There was a line of communication with the Supreme Commander, and through the Main Staff he was informed about all the information that was obtained by the security services of the Army Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it was General Tolimir's duty or his responsibility to ensure that relevant or important information, when it was deemed such by the security organs, would be transmitted to the Supreme Commander President Karadzic, despite whatever the conflict was between the political leadership and the VRS. Is that also fair to say, sir, based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is correct. That line of communication still existed, but I can't be sure of that. This is just my assumption. I was never a member of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you were never actually serving on the Main Staff. I'm asking you based on your experience in the army, based on your work with General Tolimir, based on everything that you observed, that's the basis upon which I'm asking for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you are saying. I believe that this communication went on because fighting the enemy was something that went beyond the frictions and mutual misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, based on your work with General Tolimir, your observations of General Tolimir, that communication, for example, from General Tolimir to General Karadzic would have been one that was respectful, that would have been done properly according to military discipline; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe that you can put it that way because that's how things functioned, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the about 15 minutes or so that we've got left, I want to go back a couple of years before the war, and I'm sorry to do this to you at the end of the day, but I want to get some dates firm in the record and ask you some questions about some of the command relationships that obtained pre-war and just at the beginning of the war, and then we can start fresh again tomorrow. When you were assigned to the Sibenik garrison in the 8th maritime sector, Colonel Beara was one of your superiors, you testified, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, it's been translated differently in your 2004 interview from today, and I just want the record to be a little clearer. Was he the assistant chief of the security organ at that time or the deputy chief of security, just so the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: According to our establishment, the assistant chief of security is also his deputy. That's how it has been defined by the establishment books, similarly to the fact that a chief of staff of a unit is also the deputy commander, and that's the analogy of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that was for the naval military district, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just briefly, could you describe for the Trial Chamber what geographic area that district encompassed?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the naval military district encompassed the entire territory of the Adriatic Sea, which belonged to the former state of Yugoslavia. This implies all of the islands, peninsulas, and in the depth of the territory, the area from, let's say, Pula to Balka [phoen], Kotorska, or even further down to Ulcinj. This is where the navy units of the JNA were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to define terms, is "military maritime district" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [French spoken]

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I also defined the military naval district. It was a unit of the JNA, which stood side by side with the army, the land army. It was one branch of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry if I threw you off there, sir. I started to get French interpretation in my ear, and I think maybe some other folks did as well. Let me just -- so there's no confusion on the record, is the term "military maritime district" the same as "naval district"? That's the simple question.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: A military naval district is a military unit, and this does not imply a territorial area but a military area or a military definition thereof. Just like you have the army as a branch of the military referring to the infantry, you also have a naval district, which implies certain military units, and each of these military units had its zone of responsibility in professional and military terms. This is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did the 8th maritime sector fit into the district? Was it a component of that district, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: The 8th maritime sector was a unit which was a part of the naval military district, a unit which consisted of naval forces and infantry or land forces. In organisational terms, it was a unit of the naval military district as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And so just to be clear, when Colonel Beara was one of your superior officers, he was assistant/deputy chief of the security organ for the district or for the sector?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: District.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And also while you were assigned to the 8th maritime sector, I think you testified that General Tolimir was also assigned there, and what exactly was his position at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I did not testify that General Tolimir was in the sector. He was in the naval military district if we are talking about the time when I first met him, which was sometime in 1985. At the time, he was the chief of the counterintelligence group in the naval military district. Later on, he became the chief of the security department of the Knin corps. That corps, as well, was one part of the naval military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned during your evidence-in-chief that at this time Beara was superior to Tolimir. Can you just explain to the Trial Chamber how -- why that was?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just said that Tolimir was the chief of the counterintelligence group at the time, and when he discharged those duties his superior was Naval Captain Beara. Later, when General Tolimir was re-assigned to work in the 9th corps, again, Beara was his boss because the 9th corps was also an element of the naval military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So in other words, there's nothing unusual about that; it's just the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's how things were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when did General Tolimir become security chief for the Knin corps? Do you remember? Just the year would be enough.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that because I don't remember the year. I know that in 1991, or rather, in 1992 when I first joined the corps he was there. I beginning that -- he was re-assigned at the beginning of war, but I'm sure that he was already there in 1992. Actually, I'm sure that he was there towards the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And now, moving to the Main Staff, do you have any idea when General Tolimir moved to the Main Staff? Just a year, again.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Again, I can't give you the exact date. I suppose that this was at the moment when the Army Republika Srpska was first established. I actually established a link; I put a link between these two events.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So in any case, Colonel Beara arrived at the Main Staff after General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Correct. That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at some point, sir, the security organs were separated from the intelligence organs. Do you recall what year that was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: That was in the course of 1993. That's when Naval Captain Beara was appointed chief of the security administration. Before that, there was a vacancy for that position, and I believe that it was then that the sector for intelligence and security was also established. Up to then, these two functions or positions were merged in the person of one organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then subsequently, they were separated for the remainder of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. How shall I put it? I'm trying to find the right word, if you will just bear with me. They were separated, actually. There was a change in the structure of the intelligence and the security system of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just to save a little time in the 20 minutes we've got left, before the two organs were separated, you told us that you remembered the following people being assigned as the security and intelligence department chiefs. This is before they were separated. In the 1st Krajina Corps, you recalled a person named Stevilovic, who was then succeeded by someone named Bogajevic. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I have not received the full interpretation of your question, sir. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We were having a staring contest, so I was wondering if you had. Do you recall telling us and identifying from your recollection who the various security and intelligence department chiefs were before they were separated?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in the 1st Krajina Corps, you identified a -- someone named Stevilovic, who was then succeeded by someone named Bogajevic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You identified yourself in the 2nd Krajina corps, and in the Sarajevo-Romanija corps, you identified Marko Lugonja. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is down to misinterpretation. You asked me whether I remember that. I named myself as the organ in the 2nd Krajina Corps, and Lugonja, Marko, was in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In the Eastern Bosnia corps, it was Milenko Todorovic, and in the Drina corps it was Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then when the split came, they all stayed as security chiefs, and other people took on the intelligence chief role. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as a corps command officer, you became familiar with members of the Main Staff command, is that fair to say, although you never served on the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew nearly all the generals who served on the Main Staff and some colonels, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were asked during your interview about the origin of the Main Staff, do you recall identifying the following officers, Main Staff officers who came to your mind: General Mladic, General Milovanovic, General Tolimir, General Gvero, General Djukic, and General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the page of the interview please be put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sure. It's page 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But I don't have any further questions on this issue, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but maybe Madam Fauveau still wishes to see it. All right. Can we proceed? Okay, we can proceed then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Colonel Beara, you said in your interview with the OTP that since Colonel Beara used to be General Tolimir's boss and since Colonel Beara knew General Mladic, it was only natural that he became involved in the Main Staff activities. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What can you tell the Trial Chamber about the relationship between Colonel Beara and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I think that General Mladic and Colonel Beara knew each other from the military naval district because General Mladic was for a time the Chief of Staff of the Knin Corps, which was part of the military naval district, and later on he was the commander of that corps. I think that their acquaintance started there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how would you describe the nature of their relationship in terms of professionally and how they got along? Can you give the Trial Chamber some more idea of the depth, nature of that relationship?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was a superior/subordinate relationship before everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this calls for speculation. How could the witness know about the relations between two other men?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, he could. If he doesn't, he will tell us. I mean ... Yes. In any case, you had started giving your answer saying that it was a superior subordinate relationship before everything else, and then after that, what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. I consider that their relationship was primarily of that nature in their contacts. As to their personal relationship, I assume it was good, but whether or not they were friends and so on, I couldn't tell you. I think, however, that they were on good terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about the relationship, and the same questions as I've just been asking you, between Colonel Beara and General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, for a time Naval Captain Beara was superior to Tolimir, and in wartime it was the other way around. They worked together in the service for many years, and the fact that Tolimir became Beara's superior I think did not impair their professional relationship. Such things do happen in the military, especially in wartime. Tolimir was promoted before Beara and appointed to that duty because he arrived before Beara did. Beara arrived later on, and he accepted the situation. He accepted the fact that Tolimir was now his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And beyond that professional superior/subordinate relationship, what can you tell the Trial Chamber about their personal relationship?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, their personal relationship was correct, maybe even friendly. In my contacts with both of them, I did not notice any misunderstandings or anything that would disrupt their relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to show you a document and just ask you a quick question about it before we break, and if you know anything about the subject matter, please say so. If you don't, that's okay as well. May we have 65 ter 3516, please, and I can tell you this was seized from the Croatian Ministry of Defence in 1998. And if we could look at page 6 of the document, please, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have an objection to this document because this is biographical data not supported by relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait. If you are going to give reasons for your objection, you will -- particularly the kind of reasons that you have just mentioned, I cannot let you say that or explain that in the presence of the witness. So we have two options. Either we give the pay-off to the witness and send him to the hotel, and we hear what you have to say, and then we continue tomorrow; or else we adjourn until tomorrow straightaway if you need consultation time. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can be very brief. The witness can leave, and we can put forward our arguments very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you kindly leave the courtroom, please. No, no. He is leaving and just staying outside for the time being because he said his intervention is very short. It's 5 to -- I mean, I think we can safely send him back. One moment, go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mitrovic, we are going to stop here for the day. It has been very tiring for everyone, and I thank you very much for your patience with us. We'll continue tomorrow in the afternoon. In the meantime, have a good rest, and I'm sure we'll finish tomorrow within an hour or so. Thank you. You were also given an advisory not to discuss with anyone, not to talk to anyone or discuss with anyone the subject matter of your testimony between now and tomorrow. It's a very strict order. He said something, but his microphone, is it switched on or switched off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand your warning, and I also wish you a good rest until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic, very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. First of all, the OTP has stated that this documentation was something they obtained in 1998, but it was disclosed to us only when witness Medic testified, although this documentation was not produced at the time. So that's one objection. The second objection I wish to put forward is that in this document there are incorrect details contrary to what witness Medic testified about as an investigating judge concerning the detention of Colonel Beara in connection with the incident we discussed when witness Medic testified. It would be logical for the OTP to adduce along with this the documentation which will prove that the situation was the way it's described here. There is documentation concerning this event, which in the course of the testimony of that witness we discussed here in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need this document desperately, or can you use the information that you have in there without using the document? That's my first question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I could quite literally just repeat the language that's in the document. I mean it's -- as I think I mentioned, it was just one quick question about one paragraph on the second page about him being picked up by -- personally by Generals Mladic and Tolimir on a certain occasion. I just wanted to ask if he knows anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So anyway -- I mean, because that's my hunch, but anyway, I will -- yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yeah, I know we're running out of time, but we really object to the late disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are also -- not only running out of time, but we are also violating the usual rule that one voice is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And your exception --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's Monday, 7 o'clock in the evening, and you have our permission. Come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have it as Tuesday, and thank you. Mr. President, it's the late disclosure. Ten years --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tuesday, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- ten years from when they seized the documents. Since we've been in on this case, they have not produced the document which clearly has Mr. Beara's name on it and his biography. We would just like an explanation why we weren't given this document through the course of the trial as well as the pretrial phrase. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, but that's another matter. It may not necessarily relate to its admissibility in evidence. So anyway, we'll let you fight this out between now and tomorrow morning and tomorrow afternoon, until which time we stand adjourned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
